entries.title: Utility Monster
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the revised article and matching dataset record. Focus: Nozick’s original utility-monster passage and its stated inference; the article’s hypothetical versus editorial numerical illustration; distinctions among total-utility maximizing and other consequentialist commitments; the later negative-utility variation; and reference alignment. This status records editorial traceability, not the soundness of Nozick’s objection, empirical existence of a utility monster, scholarly consensus, exhaustive literature coverage, or expert review.
entries.summary: Nozick’s primary passage in chapter 3, printed p. 41, directly supports the possibility of a utility monster who gains enormously more utility from others’ sacrifices than they lose, and his qualified claim that utilitarian theory ‘seems to require’ sacrificing everyone to increase total utility. The article now attributes this wording narrowly to Nozick, marks its 10-unit calculation as an original conditional illustration, and limits the resulting recommendation to an unrestricted additive total-utility rule under explicit assumptions. The Stanford Encyclopedia supports distinctions among classic total-utility utilitarianism and other consequentialist approaches. Chappell’s accessible Cambridge abstract distinguishes a later negative-utility variant; the full article was not accessed. The IEP entry supplies rights-based context but does not discuss Nozick’s monster. A read-only post-edit reviewer found no material corrections. The article and dataset reference URL sets match; date_verified is 2026-11-01.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Nozick presents the possibility of utility monsters that gain enormously more utility from others’ sacrifices than those others lose, and says utilitarian theory seems to require sacrifice of everyone in order to increase total utility.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Chapter 3, ‘Moral Constraints and the State,’ printed p. 41, paragraph beginning ‘Utilitarian theory is embarrassed by the possibility of utility monsters…’
claim_evidence.finding: The primary passage directly supports the description and the attribution. The article retains Nozick’s modal framing (‘possibility’) and his qualified wording (‘seems to require’) rather than presenting his conclusion as an established consequence of every maximizing theory.
claim_evidence.limitation: Only the relevant passage was read in a hosted reproduction; it establishes what Nozick wrote, not the truth of his criticism.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: added direct citation to chapter 3, p. 41, and narrowed the wording to Nozick’s stated hypothetical and inference.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The 10-unit calculation, with 1 welfare point per unit for an ordinary recipient and 100 for the monster, is an editorial illustration and favors the monster only under comparable, additive values with other effects excluded.
claim_evidence.source_title: Original editorial illustration (not a claim attributed to an external source)
claim_evidence.exact_location: Article §3, paragraph beginning ‘As a separate illustration—not Nozick’s example…’
claim_evidence.finding: No consulted source provides these numerical values. The arithmetic follows from the article’s explicit stipulations, and the revised text labels them as editorial rather than Nozick’s figures or an empirical welfare measure.
claim_evidence.limitation: The illustration does not show that interpersonal utility comparisons are measurable or morally decisive.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: explicitly identified the example as editorial and stated its comparability, additivity, and exclusion assumptions.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Nozick’s hypothetical concerns an unrestricted additive total-utility view; its implication does not automatically transfer to every consequentialist approach, including views that incorporate distribution, fairness, or priority to worse-off people.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1 on the distinct commitments composing classic utilitarianism; §3 on distributive, fairness-based, prioritarian, average, and negative-utility approaches.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP explains that total aggregation is one commitment among several and reports consequentialist alternatives that assess distribution or prioritize worse-off people. The article now avoids generalizing Nozick’s challenge to all consequentialist theories.
claim_evidence.limitation: The SEP provides a scholarly taxonomy, not proof that any proposed alternative succeeds or that Nozick’s objection is decisive.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: limited the illustrated result to an unrestricted additive total-utility rule and stated that other objectives yield different conclusions.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Chappell’s ‘negative utility monster’ is a later variation that begins from a condition of massive suffering and is distinct from Nozick’s original positive-gain case.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Publisher abstract and article record for Utilitas 33(4), pp. 417–421.
claim_evidence.finding: The abstract explicitly describes the negative variation as starting from massive suffering and identifies it as a variation on Nozick’s positive-gain monster. The article names this as Chappell’s later discussion and discloses abstract-only access.
claim_evidence.limitation: The full article’s arguments and replies were not read; only the abstract and bibliographic record were consulted.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: separated the negative-utility variation from Nozick’s original and disclosed the source access limit.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The Internet Encyclopedia entry supports context about Nozick’s rights and side-constraints but does not directly establish the utility-monster thought experiment.

entries.title: The AI Box Scenario
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the revised article and matching dataset record. Focus: who devised and participated in the 2002 role-plays; reported outcomes; the distinction between terms agreed before the trials and Yudkowsky’s later proposed protocol; how the 2012 peer-reviewed Oracle-AI article relates to the role-play; and the limits of what human role-play establishes. This status does not establish that a real AI could persuade a gatekeeper, that containment is impossible or sufficient, scholarly consensus, exhaustive literature coverage, or expert review.
entries.summary: Yudkowsky’s accessible author-hosted retrospective account says he played the AI in two 2002 text-chat trials, with Nathan Russell and David McFadzean as gatekeepers; the contemporary SL4 archive contains each gatekeeper’s report that he let the role-play AI out. Yudkowsky says the trials had no agreed rules beyond secrecy and a two-hour minimum and that his detailed public protocol was written afterward; he calls the results strictly anecdotal evidence. The Oxford repository verifies that Armstrong, Sandberg, and Bostrom later published a peer-reviewed Oracle-AI control analysis in 2012, whose Section 3 discusses Yudkowsky’s role-play; they were not participants in the trials. The article now distinguishes these sources and explicitly says no inference about actual AI capabilities is claimed. Independent read-only post-edit review found no material corrections. The five article Further Reading URLs match the dataset references, and date_verified is 2026-11-01.

sources.limitations: Retrospective first-person account, not a transcript of the private chats. Its detailed proposed protocol postdates the two trials. The author’s account and participants’ messages do not test an actual AI or establish general containment results.

entries.title: The Spandrels of San Marco
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the revised article and matching dataset record. Focus: the 1979 paper’s architectural analogy and current-utility/origin distinction; whether the authors rejected natural selection; the contested architectural terminology and Gould’s clarification of number, shape, and structural utility; attribution and definition of the later term exaptation; and publication/access qualifications. This status records traceability, not the truth of any evolutionary explanation, the prevalence of exaptation or by-products, scholarly consensus, exhaustive literature coverage, or expert review.
entries.summary: The full 1979 Gould–Lewontin paper was read in a publicly hosted reproduction, including its opening analogy and discussion of alternatives to adaptationist explanations. The Royal Society record confirms publication details and abstract, while its full text remains paywalled. The article now explains that Gould and Lewontin use the San Marco architectural spaces to illustrate why current utility alone does not establish origin, and it avoids claiming that natural selection is rejected. Gould’s full 1997 clarification supports the qualification that his byproduct claim concerned the pendentives’ necessary number and shape, not absence of structural utility, and that extending ‘spandrel’ to those 3-D structures has been debated. Gould and Vrba’s 1982 paper supports the later term exaptation and its distinction from adaptation. A read-only post-edit review found no material corrections. The four Further Reading URLs match the dataset reference URLs; date_verified is 2026-11-01.

sources.title: The spandrels of San Marco and the Panglossian paradigm: a critique of the adaptationist programme
sources.author: Stephen Jay Gould and Richard C. Lewontin
sources.publication: Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological Sciences 205(1161) (1979): 581–598; DOI 10.1098/rspb.1979.0086.
sources.source_type: Primary peer-reviewed biological and methodological argument; public scan/reproduction
sources.access_level: Complete article text was read in a publicly hosted reproduction; official publisher metadata and abstract were checked separately. This is not publisher-delivered full text.
sources.exact_locations_read: Printed pp. 581–583, abstract and §1 ‘Introduction,’ for the San Marco example, the necessary four spaces and tapering form, the use of mosaics, and the distinction between current utility and reasons for origin; pp. 589–592 and the abstract for the authors’ pluralistic account, natural selection as one process among others, and alternatives to adaptationist explanations.
sources.limitations: The full-text reproduction is hosted by a third party; its front matter reproduces JSTOR copyright text and its OCR can contain errors. The Royal Society states that its own web text is OCR-derived and that publisher full text is available only by purchase/institutional access. The audit did not consult San Marco architectural archives or independently establish original architects’ intentions.

sources.access_level: Official publisher page, bibliographic details, and abstract were read; full article was paywalled.
sources.exact_locations_read: Publisher citation and publication history; abstract passages identifying the failure to distinguish current utility from origin, the need to consider alternatives, and the authors’ support for Darwin’s pluralistic approach.
sources.limitations: The abstract is not a substitute for full-text passages; the full text was instead accessed through a third-party-hosted reproduction. The page warns that its online abstract was generated from OCR and may contain errors.

sources.title: The exaptive excellence of spandrels as a term and prototype
sources.author: Stephen Jay Gould
sources.publication: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 94(20) (1997): 10750–10755.
sources.source_type: Primary author clarification and scholarly response
sources.access_level: The full article in PubMed Central was retrieved and relevant passages were read; not every citation or all discussion of the debate was independently followed.
sources.exact_locations_read: Abstract; section ‘Claim One: What’s in a Name?’ on the use of ‘spandrel’ for San Marco’s pendentives and objections to the terminology; section ‘Claim Two: Are Spandrels Spandrels or Adaptations?’ on structural utility and Gould’s intended properties of number and shape as by-products of the dome-on-four-arches design.
sources.limitations: This is Gould’s later clarification and response, not an independent architectural consensus statement or a substitute for the 1979 article. It acknowledges disagreement rather than resolving architectural usage for all specialists.

sources.title: Exaptation—a missing term in the science of form
sources.author: Stephen Jay Gould and Elisabeth S. Vrba
sources.access_level: The full paper text was retrieved; the abstract and relevant sections were read, not every example or later citation.
sources.exact_locations_read: Abstract; §II, ‘Two Meanings of Adaptation’; §III, ‘A Definition of Exaptation,’ especially printed pp. 6–7, defining useful characters evolved for another use or no function and later co-opted for a current role.
sources.limitations: This 1982 paper supports the later terminology and its authorship, not the wording of the 1979 paper. Its definitions reflect the authors’ proposed terminology and do not eliminate all later debate about adaptation concepts.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Gould and Lewontin use San Marco’s dome and mosaics to illustrate that the spaces’ present decorative use does not establish that the spaces originated in order to house that artwork; the article is an analogy and methodological argument, not a strict hypothetical experiment.
claim_evidence.source_title: The spandrels of San Marco and the Panglossian paradigm: a critique of the adaptationist programme
claim_evidence.exact_location: Abstract and §1, ‘Introduction,’ printed pp. 581–583; especially the passage on the architectural constraint, fit of the mosaics, and ‘Spandrels do not exist to house the evangelists.’
claim_evidence.finding: The primary paper directly supports the analogy and its point about reversing causal explanation from present fit. The revised article labels it an analogy and methodological argument rather than a controlled or strict hypothetical experiment.
claim_evidence.limitation: The architectural example is the authors’ account. The audit did not independently verify building chronology, the original architects’ intentions, or the historical sequence of mosaic placement through archival evidence.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced a generic architectural setup with the specific number/shape and later-mosaic account, and qualified the status of the example.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The 1979 critique does not claim that natural selection never operates; it criticizes adaptationist explanations that treat current utility as sufficient evidence of origin and calls for a pluralistic account of evolutionary change.
claim_evidence.source_title: The spandrels of San Marco and the Panglossian paradigm: a critique of the adaptationist programme
claim_evidence.exact_location: Abstract, printed pp. 581–582; §4, ‘The Master’s Voice Re-examined,’ printed pp. 589–590; §5, ‘A Partial Typology of Alternatives to the Adaptationist Programme,’ beginning p. 590.
claim_evidence.finding: The authors explicitly support Darwin’s pluralistic approach and describe natural selection as a force that may mediate change, while arguing for attention to developmental constraints and non-adaptive alternatives. The article does not attribute rejection of selection to them.
claim_evidence.limitation: The paper’s theoretical position and its assessment of competing explanations are the authors’ argument, not an established consensus about the prevalence of by-products.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: explicitly states that the authors do not reject selection and summarizes their critique as a call for pluralistic explanations.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Gould later clarified that the intended byproduct properties are the pendentives’ necessary number and shape, regardless of structural utility; extending ‘spandrel’ to three-dimensional pendentives has been disputed.
claim_evidence.source_title: The exaptive excellence of spandrels as a term and prototype
claim_evidence.exact_location: ‘Claim One: What’s in a Name?’ and ‘Claim Two: Are Spandrels Spandrels or Adaptations?’; Gould’s discussion of pendentives, their four-in-number/roughly triangular form, and structural uses such as buttressing.
claim_evidence.finding: Gould explicitly acknowledges that most architects apparently do not use ‘spandrel’ for these 3-D structures, notes some architectural-historical usage, and defines his intended claim as the necessary number and shape arising from the chosen dome-on-four-arches design. He says the pendentives can still have structural utility.
claim_evidence.limitation: This establishes Gould’s clarification and that terminology was contested; it does not show that all architects accept his terminology or settle the issue independently.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: qualified the word ‘spandrel’ and preserved Gould’s distinction between byproduct form/number and structural usefulness.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Gould and Vrba introduced ‘exaptation’ in 1982 for a useful character co-opted for its current role after evolving for another use or for no function.
claim_evidence.source_title: Exaptation—a missing term in the science of form
claim_evidence.exact_location: Abstract and §III, ‘A Definition of Exaptation,’ printed pp. 6–7.
claim_evidence.finding: The primary 1982 paper explicitly proposes the term and defines the relevant historical distinction. The revised article no longer describes exaptation as a field of study or attributes the term to the 1979 paper.
claim_evidence.limitation: The term is later than the 1979 critique and reflects the authors’ proposed taxonomy; the article uses it as later terminology rather than as Gould and Lewontin’s own label in 1979.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: attributed the term to Gould and Vrba (1982) and distinguished later co-option from the original byproduct analogy.

unresolved: The Royal Society full text was paywalled; the full 1979 article was read through a third-party-hosted reproduction whose OCR may contain errors.
The original architects’ intentions and the building’s detailed history were not independently checked against architectural archives; the article attributes the analogy to Gould and Lewontin.
The audit does not establish how common exaptations or non-adaptive by-products are in biological systems or settle the architectural terminology debate.
entries.post_edit_review: Independent read-only review found no material corrections; it checked geometry, the current-use/origin distinction, natural-selection framing, terminology qualification, exaptation attribution, and article/dataset URL alignment.
